summary.text:
Paragraph 36 is the reason to write. Chorley reports its 2025/26 investment yield as 3.29% and says plainly how it got there — "dividing the total percentages by the four investment types". Weighting those same four rates by the average balances in the same table gives 3.876%. The council is understating its own performance by roughly 59 basis points, because a £439k Barclays call account at 1.38% carries the same weight as £6.45m of money market funds at 4.08%.

Second, the book. Fifteen PWLB loans totalling £62.987m, published in full with loan numbers, dates, rates and profiles — one of very few councils that does. Nearly half of it is a single £28.277m annuity at 1.87% running to 2059. Every one of the fifteen prices below par today, about £22.0m in total, and it is the only book in the library with no loan in premium at all.

£20m of the £83.593m is short-term local authority money and no new long-term PWLB was taken. Financing costs are 19.07% of net revenue stream against a 17.69% estimate.

Three officers published with addresses.

officer.reconciliation: Appendix A's fifteen loans sum to £62,987k exactly and we hold all fifteen at a balance of £62,258,577. The reported 3.29% reproduces as the simple average of the four stated rates; the balance-weighted figure from the same table is 3.876%.
officer.body:
Hi Hanne,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Audit and Governance on 22 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. Your Appendix A publishes the whole loan schedule — loan numbers, start and maturity dates, rates and repayment profiles — which very few councils do and which makes the report far more useful than most. The fifteen rows sum to £62,987k exactly, and we hold all fifteen at a balance of £62,258,577, the difference being four and a half months of amortisation on the annuity and EIP loans.

The reason we wrote is paragraph 36, and it is in your favour rather than against you.

You report the 2025/26 investment yield as 3.29% and you say openly how it is calculated: "dividing the total percentages by the four investment types". Taking the same four rates from the same table and weighting them by the average balances alongside them gives 3.876% — (4,293 × 3.85 + 439 × 1.38 + 3,024 × 3.84 + 6,450 × 4.08) ÷ 14,206.

The gap is about 59 basis points, and it exists because a £439k Barclays call account at 1.38% is given exactly the same weight as £6.45m of money market funds at 4.08%. On a simple average, the smallest and worst-performing balance in the portfolio pulls the headline down as hard as the largest and best. So the number that goes to committee understates what the treasury function actually earned.

We raise it because it is the sort of thing that only shows up when you read a lot of these side by side, and because the direction matters: most councils quote a balance-weighted figure, so a 3.29% next to their 4.0-odd percents reads as underperformance when on a like-for-like basis it is not. Chorley's weighted 3.88% sits comfortably against the sector. We have no view on which basis you should use — that is yours — and paragraph 36 is admirably clear about the method, which is more than most reports manage.

One caveat on our own working, because we would rather flag it than not. The earnings column in Table 8 does not reproduce the stated yields either — £190k on £4,293k is 4.43% against the 3.85% shown, for instance — so the three columns appear to be on slightly different bases. Our 3.876% uses only your balances and your stated rates, which we think is the defensible calculation, but you will know what sits behind the earnings column better than we can.

On the borrowing side there is nothing to do and we are not suggesting otherwise. Almost the whole book is 2013 to 2022 money — a single £28.277m annuity at 1.87% running to 2059 is nearly half of it, and there is a £10m maturity loan at 2.02% out to 2072. On the DMO's premature repayment curve today all fifteen loans price below par, about £22.0m in total. Yours is the only book we have priced this year with no loan in premium at all. Standard caveats and we mean them: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

For the £20m of short-term local authority borrowing inside the £83.593m: July's PWLB lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is thin, and thin PWLB months are when inter-authority money gets dear. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four fit Chorley. Reading the Metrics dashboard is the one that speaks to the weighting question and how the sector reports these numbers. Money Market Funds (CNAV / LVNAV / VNAV) for where two-fifths of the balance sits. PWLB repayment structures, given how much of your book is annuity and EIP rather than maturity. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
